body_markdown:
Shigella infections are a growing health concern in the US, with drug-resistant cases complicating treatment. Learn about symptoms, transmission, prevention and when to seek medical care.


Shigella infections are becoming an increasing public health concern in the United States, particularly as antibiotic-resistant strains make some cases more difficult to treat. The bacterial infection, known as shigellosis, can cause diarrhoea, stomach cramps, fever and other gastrointestinal symptoms. In severe cases, it may lead to dehydration and serious complications.


According to figures cited in a report published by *The Independent* on 9 October 2026, approximately 450,000 Shigella infections occur in the US each year, with around 38 deaths annually. The report also highlights the challenge posed by drug-resistant infections, which limit the effectiveness of commonly prescribed antibiotics.


Although Shigella is commonly associated with contaminated food and water, it can also spread through sexual contact involving exposure to faecal matter. Understanding how the bacteria spreads, recognising the symptoms and following appropriate prevention measures are essential to reducing transmission.


## What Is Shigella and Why Is It a Growing Concern?


Shigella is a group of bacteria that causes an intestinal infection called shigellosis. It spreads easily between people, meaning even small amounts of contaminated material can contribute to transmission.


The infection can affect people of different ages, although some groups face a greater risk of serious illness. Young children, people with limited access to clean water and sanitation, and individuals exposed through particular sexual activities may be especially vulnerable.


One of the biggest concerns is the growing prevalence of antibiotic-resistant Shigella. Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria develop the ability to survive medicines that would normally kill them or prevent their growth.


This creates additional challenges for healthcare professionals, particularly when patients develop severe symptoms or require treatment for infections that do not respond to standard antibiotics.


## Shigella Cases and Antibiotic Resistance in the US


The scale of Shigella infections highlights the importance of continued public health monitoring. Estimates cited in the October 2026 report suggest that hundreds of thousands of infections occur annually across the country.


The report references US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) data indicating that approximately 242,000 people experience drug-resistant Shigella infections each year.


These figures demonstrate why antibiotic resistance is an important concern. When a bacterial infection becomes resistant to commonly used medicines, clinicians may have fewer effective treatment options available.


An especially concerning development is the spread of extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Shigella. According to the report, there is no government-approved oral antibiotic available for treating this form of infection. The precise proportion of annual resistant cases caused by XDR strains remains unclear.


Researchers and public health officials have therefore emphasised the importance of antibiotic susceptibility testing, timely reporting and continued surveillance. These measures can help healthcare professionals understand which treatments may work and monitor the spread of resistant bacteria.


## Common Symptoms of Shigella Infection


Shigellosis primarily affects the digestive system, and symptoms can range from mild gastrointestinal discomfort to severe illness.


Common symptoms include:


- Diarrhoea, which may contain blood.
- Abdominal pain and stomach cramps.
- Fever.
- Nausea and vomiting.
- Dehydration caused by fluid loss.


In more serious cases, complications can include dysentery and, rarely, seizures or bloodstream infections. Severe illness may be particularly dangerous for young children and people who are more vulnerable to infection.


Anyone experiencing bloody diarrhoea, signs of significant dehydration, persistent vomiting or worsening symptoms should seek prompt medical advice. Severe symptoms may require urgent medical assessment.


It is also important to remember that not every episode of diarrhoea is caused by Shigella. Other infections and medical conditions can produce similar symptoms, so an appropriate clinical assessment may be necessary to establish the cause.


## How Does Shigella Spread?


Shigella spreads when bacteria enter the mouth, usually through contaminated hands, food, water or objects. Because the infection can spread through very small amounts of faecal contamination, everyday hygiene practices play a significant role in prevention.


Transmission may occur when someone touches a contaminated surface and then touches their mouth, consumes contaminated food or drinks unsafe water.


Sexual contact can also contribute to transmission, particularly activities involving direct or indirect exposure to faecal matter. Public health guidance has highlighted increased risks among men who have sex with men, although the infection is not limited to any particular group.


The October 2026 report also references UK research indicating that sexual transmission of Shigella increased faster annually than other transmission routes between 2015 and 2020.


These findings underline the importance of providing clear, non-judgemental health information. Shigella is an infectious disease, and prevention depends on awareness, hygiene, access to healthcare and appropriate precautions rather than assumptions about an individual's identity.


## Who Is Most at Risk?


Shigella can affect anyone, but certain circumstances increase the likelihood of infection or more serious outcomes.


**Young children:** Children under five are at greater risk of complications from Shigella, including illness caused by drug-resistant strains.


**People exposed through sexual contact:** Sexual activities involving exposure to faecal matter can facilitate transmission.


**People with limited access to sanitation:** Individuals experiencing homelessness or lacking reliable access to clean water and toilets may face increased exposure risks.


**People exposed to contaminated water or food:** Drinking unsafe water, eating contaminated food or swimming in contaminated water can provide opportunities for infection.


These risk factors do not mean that everyone in these groups will become infected. They highlight circumstances in which prevention, symptom awareness and access to appropriate healthcare are particularly important.


## Treatment Options for Shigella


Many people recover from Shigella infection with supportive care, including adequate fluid intake and oral rehydration solutions when appropriate. Replacing lost fluids and electrolytes is particularly important when diarrhoea is frequent.


However, some infections can become severe and may require medical treatment. Antibiotics may be considered in selected cases to help reduce the severity or duration of illness, depending on the patient's condition and the susceptibility of the bacteria.


Drug resistance complicates these decisions. If the bacteria are resistant to a prescribed antibiotic, that medicine may not work as intended. Healthcare professionals may therefore recommend stool testing and antibiotic susceptibility testing to guide treatment.


People should not take leftover antibiotics or self-prescribe medication for suspected Shigella infection. The appropriate treatment depends on individual circumstances, and unnecessary antibiotic use can contribute to the wider problem of antimicrobial resistance.


There is currently no routinely available vaccine for Shigella infection. Nevertheless, vaccine research continues, and the October 2026 report describes promising early findings from a candidate vaccine study involving US adults. Further research is needed before such findings can establish the vaccine's effectiveness and availability for wider use.


## How to Prevent Shigella Infection


Simple hygiene measures can help reduce the risk of Shigella transmission.


- **Wash your hands thoroughly:** Use soap and water for at least 20 seconds, especially before eating, after using the toilet and after changing nappies.
- **Practise safer food handling:** Keep food preparation areas clean and avoid consuming food or water that may be contaminated.
- **Take care around sexual activity:** Avoid sexual contact when you or a partner has diarrhoea or has recently recovered. The source article advises waiting at least two weeks after diarrhoea has resolved.
- **Maintain good personal hygiene:** Clean contaminated surfaces and wash your hands carefully after activities that could involve exposure to faecal matter.
- **Seek medical advice when necessary:** Persistent, bloody or severe diarrhoea should not be ignored, especially when accompanied by dehydration or fever.


People diagnosed with Shigella should follow advice from their healthcare professional and local public health authorities about recovery, hygiene and reducing the risk of passing the infection to others.


## Conclusion


Rising Shigella infections and the spread of antibiotic-resistant strains present important challenges for public health in the United States. With hundreds of thousands of estimated infections each year, improving awareness of symptoms, transmission and prevention remains essential.


Although many people recover with supportive care, severe infections and drug-resistant bacteria can make treatment more complicated. Good hand hygiene, safer food and water practices, appropriate sexual health precautions and timely medical assessment can all help reduce transmission.


As antibiotic resistance continues to attract attention, ongoing surveillance, responsible antibiotic use and further research into potential vaccines will remain important parts of the response.
